units.title: How to Look at Art
units.blurb: Formal analysis, subject and style, the media of painting and sculpture, patrons, and how works are dated and attributed.

units.title: Prehistoric Art
units.blurb: Cave paintings, carved figures and the great stone monuments.

units.title: The Ancient Near East and Egypt
units.blurb: Mesopotamia, Assyria and Persia; the rules of Egyptian art; pyramids, temples and the tomb of Tutankhamun.

units.title: The Aegean, Greece and Rome
units.blurb: Minoan and Mycenaean art, Greek vases, the orders, the Parthenon, sculpture from Archaic to Hellenistic, and Roman building and portraits.

units.title: Early Christian and Byzantine Art
units.blurb: Basilicas, the mosaics of Ravenna, Hagia Sophia and icons.

units.title: Islamic Art and Architecture
units.blurb: Mosques and their parts, geometric ornament, arabesque and calligraphy, and the Alhambra.

units.title: Medieval Europe
units.blurb: Illuminated manuscripts, Romanesque and Gothic churches, stained glass and the Books of Hours.

units.title: Asia, Africa and the Americas before 1500
units.blurb: Chinese landscape painting and ceramics, Japanese and Buddhist art, Ife, Benin and Great Zimbabwe, and the Olmec, Maya, Aztec and Inca.

units.title: The Renaissance
units.blurb: Giotto, perspective and Brunelleschi's dome; Leonardo, Raphael and Michelangelo; Venice; Van Eyck, Dürer and Bruegel; Mannerism.

topics.title: Formal Analysis: Describe, Analyze, Interpret
topics.short: Formal analysis looks at how a work is made, its line, color, light, composition and scale, before asking what it means.
topics.trouble: People jump to the story or the artist's life and never describe what is in front of them. Description is the evidence for everything else.

topics.title: Subject, Genre and Style
topics.short: The subject is what a work shows; genres group subjects (portrait, landscape, still life, history painting, genre scene); style is how it is shown.
topics.trouble: People use "genre painting" for any type of painting. In art history a genre scene is a picture of everyday life.

topics.title: Fresco, Tempera, Oil and More
topics.short: True fresco is painted into wet plaster; egg tempera dries fast in fine strokes; oil paint dries slowly and allows glazes and blending.
topics.trouble: People call any wall painting a fresco. True (buon) fresco is painted on wet plaster; Leonardo's Last Supper is not a true fresco, and that is part of why it decayed.

topics.title: Carving, Modeling and Casting
topics.short: Sculptors carve (take away from stone or wood), model (build up clay or wax) or cast (pour metal into a mold). Relief stays attached to a background; sculpture in the round does not.
topics.trouble: People think bronze statues are carved. Bronze is cast, usually by the lost-wax process.

topics.title: Patrons and Context
topics.short: Most art before modern times was commissioned: rulers, churches, guilds and families paid for it and often set its subject, size and materials.
topics.trouble: People picture every artist as a lone genius painting for himself. For most of history, art was made to order.

topics.title: Dating and Attribution
topics.short: Dates and artists come from documents, signatures, style and science. "c." means about; "attributed to" means scholars think so but it is not certain.
topics.trouble: People read "c. 1500" as an exact year, or "attributed to" as proven. Both labels tell you how sure scholars are.

topics.title: Cave Paintings
topics.short: Paleolithic people painted animals deep in caves: Chauvet more than 30,000 years ago and Lascaux about 17,000 years ago, with mineral pigments and charcoal.
topics.trouble: People imagine cave art as crude scribbles. The animals are observed closely and often use the bumps of the rock for form.

topics.title: Carved Figures
topics.short: Small carvings in ivory, bone and stone are among the oldest art. The Lion-Man of Hohlenstein-Stadel, carved from mammoth ivory, is about 40,000 years old.
topics.trouble: People assume the oldest art is painting. Carved figures are at least as old.

topics.title: Stonehenge and the Megaliths
topics.short: Neolithic people raised huge stones into circles and tombs. Stonehenge was built in stages from about 3000 to 1500 BC.
topics.trouble: People credit the Druids with Stonehenge. It was built more than a thousand years before the Druids are recorded.

topics.title: Mesopotamia: Ziggurats and Steles
topics.short: Sumer and Babylon built mud-brick ziggurats and carved steles; the Stele of Hammurabi (about 1750 BC) shows the king before the god Shamash above his laws.
topics.trouble: People mix up a ziggurat with an Egyptian pyramid. A ziggurat is a stepped platform with a temple on top, not a tomb.

topics.title: Assyria, Babylon and Persia
topics.short: Assyrian palaces had guardian lamassu and carved reliefs; Babylon's Ishtar Gate (about 575 BC) glowed with glazed brick; Persepolis shows rows of tribute bearers.
topics.trouble: People think a lamassu has four legs. Seen from the side and front together, many have five, so they look complete from either view.

topics.title: The Rules of Egyptian Art
topics.short: Egyptian artists showed people in composite view (head and legs in profile, eye and shoulders from the front), used hierarchical scale, and laid out figures on a grid.
topics.trouble: People think Egyptians couldn't draw realistically. The rules showed each part in its clearest view on purpose, and they lasted three thousand years.

topics.title: Pyramids and the Old Kingdom
topics.short: The pyramids of Giza (about 2600 to 2500 BC) were royal tombs. The Great Sphinx, probably made for King Khafre, guards the way to his pyramid.
topics.trouble: People think slaves built the pyramids. Evidence from the workers' town and tombs points to organized crews who were housed and fed, not slaves.

topics.title: Temples and the New Kingdom
topics.short: New Kingdom pharaohs built great temples like Karnak and Hatshepsut's at Deir el-Bahari; the Amarna period brought the bust of Nefertiti, and Tutankhamun's tomb its gold mask.
topics.trouble: People think Tutankhamun was a great pharaoh because his tomb is famous. He was a young king; his tomb is famous because it was found nearly intact in 1922.

topics.title: Minoan and Mycenaean Art
topics.short: Minoan Crete built palaces like Knossos and painted lively sea creatures on pottery; Mycenae is known for walls of huge stones and gold masks.
topics.trouble: People think the Mask of Agamemnon belonged to Agamemnon. It is older than the Trojan War of legend; the name came from its finder, Heinrich Schliemann.

topics.title: Greek Vases: Black-Figure and Red-Figure
topics.short: In black-figure, figures are painted black on the red clay; in red-figure, about 530 BC on, the background is painted black and figures stay red, so details can be painted with a brush.
topics.trouble: People mix the two up. Ask what color the figures are: black figures on red ground, or red figures on black ground.

topics.title: The Doric, Ionic and Corinthian Orders
topics.short: Doric columns have plain cushion capitals and no base; Ionic capitals have scrolls (volutes); Corinthian capitals have acanthus leaves.
topics.trouble: People mix up Ionic and Corinthian. Scrolls are Ionic; leaves are Corinthian.

topics.title: The Parthenon
topics.short: Built on the Athenian Acropolis from 447 to 432 BC, the Parthenon is a Doric temple to Athena, designed by Iktinos and Kallikrates with sculpture overseen by Phidias.
topics.trouble: People think the Parthenon is built of perfectly straight lines. Its floor curves upward and its columns swell and lean slightly, refinements that make it look straight.

topics.title: Greek Sculpture: Archaic to Classical
topics.short: Greek sculpture moved from the stiff, smiling figures of the Archaic period to the natural poses of the Classical, like the bronze Charioteer of Delphi.
topics.trouble: People think Greek statues were always white marble. They were painted in bright colors; most of the paint has worn away.

topics.title: Contrapposto and the Hellenistic Age
topics.short: Contrapposto puts the weight on one leg so hips and shoulders tilt; Hellenistic sculpture after 323 BC added drama and motion, as in the Winged Victory of Samothrace.
topics.trouble: People think contrapposto only means a bent knee. It is the whole body's shift of weight, with hips and shoulders tilting opposite ways.

topics.title: Roman Arches, Concrete and Domes
topics.short: Romans used the round arch, the vault and concrete to build aqueducts like the Pont du Gard, the Colosseum and the domed Pantheon.
topics.trouble: People think Romans only copied Greek temples. Concrete, arches and vaults let them build interior spaces the Greeks never did.

topics.title: Roman Portraits and Wall Painting
topics.short: Republican portraits show age and wrinkles (verism); wall paintings at Pompeii and the Villa of Livia open walls into gardens and views.
topics.trouble: People think the Romans painted only flat walls. Their wall paintings used shading and overlapping to suggest depth, centuries before the Renaissance.

topics.title: Early Christian Art and the Basilica
topics.short: After AD 313, Christians built basilicas, long halls with an apse at one end, borrowed from Roman public buildings.
topics.trouble: People think a basilica is a religious building in origin. The Romans used basilicas as law courts and meeting halls first.

topics.title: The Mosaics of Ravenna
topics.short: At San Vitale in Ravenna (about AD 547), glittering mosaics of glass and stone show the emperor Justinian and the empress Theodora with their courts.
topics.trouble: People expect the figures to look solid. Byzantine mosaics flatten figures and float them on gold to show a heavenly, timeless world.

topics.title: Hagia Sophia
topics.short: Built in Constantinople in five years, AD 532 to 537, by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, Hagia Sophia set a huge dome on pendentives over a square plan.
topics.trouble: People think the minarets are part of the original church. They were added after 1453, when it became a mosque.

topics.title: Icons
topics.short: An icon is a holy image painted on wood, often in egg tempera with gold. Icons follow set types, so faces and poses repeat across centuries.
topics.trouble: People judge icons as failed realism. Their makers aimed at sameness and spiritual presence, not likeness.

topics.title: The Mosque and Its Parts
topics.short: A mosque's prayer hall faces Mecca; the qibla wall holds the mihrab niche, the minbar is the pulpit, and a minaret calls to prayer. The Dome of the Rock (691) is among the oldest Islamic monuments.
topics.trouble: People think every mosque has a dome and four minarets. Plans vary widely: hypostyle halls, courtyards with iwans, central domes.

topics.title: Geometry, Arabesque and Calligraphy
topics.short: Islamic art is famous for interlaced geometric patterns, arabesque (flowing vine scrolls) and calligraphy, the most honored art.
topics.trouble: People think Islamic art has no images of people at all. Religious settings generally avoid them, but palaces, manuscripts and ceramics often show figures.

topics.title: Córdoba and the Alhambra
topics.short: In Spain, the Great Mosque of Córdoba (begun 785) has rows of striped double arches; the Alhambra palaces of Granada (mostly 14th century) have carved stucco and muqarnas vaults.
topics.trouble: People think the Alhambra is a mosque. It is a palace and fortress of the Nasrid rulers.

topics.title: Carpets, Lamps and Books
topics.short: Luxury arts carried Islamic design across the world: knotted carpets like the Ardabil carpet (1539–40), enameled glass mosque lamps and illustrated manuscripts.
topics.trouble: People think these were minor crafts. In the Islamic world, textiles, metalwork and books were among the most prized arts.

topics.title: Illuminated Manuscripts
topics.short: Monks copied and decorated books by hand. The Book of Kells (about 800) and the Lindisfarne Gospels (about 715) fill pages with knotwork and interlace.
topics.trouble: People call the whole Middle Ages the "Dark Ages," when nothing of value was made. Books like these are among the most intricate art ever made.

topics.title: Romanesque Churches
topics.short: Romanesque churches (about 1000 to 1150) have thick walls, round arches, barrel vaults and small windows, and carved portals for pilgrims.
topics.trouble: People think "Romanesque" means built by the Romans. It means "in the Roman manner": round arches and heavy masonry, a thousand years later.

topics.title: Gothic Cathedrals
topics.short: Gothic builders, from about 1140, combined pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses to raise tall, thin walls filled with glass.
topics.trouble: People think the Goths built Gothic churches. The name was a later insult from Renaissance writers who thought the style barbaric.

topics.title: Stained Glass
topics.short: Pieces of colored glass held in lead strips filled Gothic windows with light and stories; Chartres and the Sainte-Chapelle (1240s) are famous for it.
topics.trouble: People think the glass was painted all over. The color is in the glass; painters added only lines and shading in a dark glass paint, fired on.

topics.title: Books of Hours and the Late Middle Ages
topics.short: Wealthy owners ordered prayer books with calendar pictures, like the Limbourg brothers' Très Riches Heures (about 1412 to 1416) for the Duke of Berry.
topics.trouble: People think medieval art ignored daily life. The calendar pages show feasts, farming and castles season by season.

topics.title: Chinese Landscape Painting
topics.short: Song dynasty painters such as Fan Kuan (about 1000) and Guo Xi (1072) painted towering mountains in ink on silk, on hanging scrolls and handscrolls.
topics.trouble: People expect one fixed viewpoint. Chinese landscapes use shifting viewpoints, so you wander through the mountains rather than look from one spot.

topics.title: Bronzes, Clay Soldiers and Porcelain
topics.short: Shang dynasty ritual bronzes (about 1600 to 1046 BC), the Terracotta Army of the first emperor (about 210 BC) and Ming blue-and-white porcelain span three thousand years.
topics.trouble: People think the Terracotta soldiers came from one mold. Their faces, hair and armor vary; workshops combined mold-made parts with hand modeling.

topics.title: Buddhist Art Across Asia
topics.short: Buddhist art spread from India across Asia: stupas, robed Buddha figures from Gandhara and Mathura, and temples like Japan's Byōdō-in (1053).
topics.trouble: People think the Buddha was always shown in human form. Early Buddhist art often showed him through symbols, such as footprints, a tree or a wheel.

topics.title: Heian Japan and the Tale of Genji
topics.short: Heian court art includes the Phoenix Hall of the Byōdō-in and the 12th-century Tale of Genji handscrolls, seen from above with the roofs "blown off."
topics.trouble: People read a handscroll like a book page. It is unrolled a section at a time, right to left.

topics.title: Temples of South and Southeast Asia
topics.short: Hindu temples rise like sacred mountains: the Brihadishvara at Thanjavur (completed 1010) and Angkor Wat in Cambodia (12th century).
topics.trouble: People think Angkor Wat was always Buddhist. It was built as a Hindu temple to Vishnu and later became a Buddhist site.

topics.title: Nok, Ife, Benin and Great Zimbabwe
topics.short: Nok terracottas (more than 2,000 years old), the naturalistic Ife heads (12th to 15th centuries), Benin's brass plaques and Great Zimbabwe's stone walls show many African traditions.
topics.trouble: People think of "African art" as one timeless style. Africa's arts have many cultures, dates, named workshops and histories.

topics.title: Olmec, Maya and Aztec
topics.short: The Olmec carved colossal basalt heads (about 1200 to 900 BC); the Maya built Palenque and wrote in glyphs; the Aztec carved the great Sun Stone (about 1502 to 1520).
topics.trouble: People call the Aztec Sun Stone a working calendar. It carries calendar signs, but scholars debate its use; it may have been a ceremonial altar or a monument to the sun.

topics.title: The Andes and Ancient North America
topics.short: The Inca fitted stones without mortar at Machu Picchu (about 1450); the Moche made portrait vessels; Ancestral Puebloans built Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde (about 1190 to 1260).
topics.trouble: People think ancient America had no great builders. Inca masonry, Puebloan cliff dwellings and Mississippian mounds say otherwise.

topics.title: Giotto and the New Naturalism
topics.short: In the Arena Chapel in Padua (about 1305), Giotto painted solid, weighty figures with real feeling, a break from flat Byzantine style.
topics.trouble: People think the Renaissance began suddenly in 1400. Giotto's solid figures a century earlier pointed the way.

topics.title: Linear Perspective
topics.short: Brunelleschi showed how lines going back meet at one vanishing point (about 1415 to 1420), Alberti wrote the method down (1435), and Masaccio used it in paint.
topics.trouble: People think no one showed depth before the Renaissance. Roman painters suggested depth by eye; the Renaissance made a mathematical system.

topics.title: Brunelleschi's Dome
topics.short: Filippo Brunelleschi raised the dome of Florence Cathedral from 1420 to 1436 without full wooden centering, using a double shell and herringbone brick.
topics.trouble: People think the dome is held up by buttresses. It has none; its double shell, ribs and brick patterns carry it.

topics.title: Early Renaissance Sculpture and Painting
topics.short: Ghiberti's Gates of Paradise, Donatello's bronze Gattamelata, Fra Angelico's Annunciation and Piero della Francesca's portraits brought the new realism to Florence and beyond.
topics.trouble: People mix up Ghiberti's doors with a painting. They are gilded bronze reliefs that use perspective in metal.

topics.title: Leonardo da Vinci
topics.short: Leonardo painted the Last Supper (about 1495 to 1498) and the Mona Lisa (begun about 1503), using sfumato, soft smoky transitions without hard outlines.
topics.trouble: People think Leonardo finished many paintings. Fewer than twenty survive, and several were left unfinished.

topics.title: Raphael and Michelangelo
topics.short: Raphael painted calm, graceful portraits and frescoes in Rome; Michelangelo was a sculptor, painter and architect who designed the dome of St. Peter's.
topics.trouble: People think Michelangelo was mainly a painter. He called himself a sculptor, and late in life he worked mostly as an architect.

topics.title: Venice: Color and Light
topics.short: Venetian painters such as Giovanni Bellini and Titian built pictures from rich color and oil glazes rather than line, painting on canvas in the damp lagoon air.
topics.trouble: People think Florence and Venice painted the same way. Florence prized drawing (disegno); Venice prized color (colorito).

topics.title: Van Eyck and Northern Oil Painting
topics.short: Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait (1434) shows what oil glazes could do: tiny details, glowing color and a convex mirror reflecting the room.
topics.trouble: People think Van Eyck invented oil paint. Oil was known before him; he and other Netherlandish painters perfected layered glazes.

topics.title: Dürer and the Print
topics.short: Albrecht Dürer of Nuremberg made woodcuts and engravings that sold across Europe, like his Rhinoceros (1515), and watercolors such as the Young Hare (1502).
topics.trouble: People mix up woodcut and engraving. A woodcut prints the raised parts of a carved block; an engraving prints ink held in lines cut into metal.

topics.title: Bruegel and Everyday Life
topics.short: Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted peasants, seasons and landscapes, such as Hunters in the Snow and The Harvesters (both 1565).
topics.trouble: People think Bruegel was a peasant painting his own village. He was an educated city artist whose patrons were wealthy collectors.

topics.title: Renaissance Architecture
topics.short: Renaissance architects revived Roman columns, round arches and domes with clear proportions; Palladio's Villa La Rotonda (begun about 1567) was copied for centuries.
topics.trouble: People mix Renaissance and Gothic façades. Renaissance buildings use symmetry, round arches and classical orders; Gothic ones use pointed arches.

topics.title: Mannerism and the Late Renaissance
topics.short: After about 1520, Mannerist artists stretched proportions, crowded space and used cool, strange colors; Bronzino's portraits and El Greco's View of Toledo show the range.
topics.trouble: People think Mannerist distortion was a lack of skill. These artists could draw "correctly" and chose elegance and strangeness on purpose.
